vignette:
Kwame is a 25-year-old journalist who came to the United States from Ghana three years ago for a fellowship. He now lives with his girlfriend in a small apartment in a busy city, and he works as a reporter covering local politics. Eight months ago, while walking home late from an assignment, he was stopped by police officers who mistook him for a suspect in a recent robbery. They ordered him to the ground at gunpoint, handcuffed him, and held him face-down on the concrete for nearly twenty minutes before a supervisor arrived and confirmed his identity was clean. The officers apologized and drove him home, but the memory of those minutes-the heavy footsteps behind him before the shout, the cold metal of the handcuffs, the sound of a police radio crackling with static-has not faded. When he tries to tell his girlfriend what happened, he loses the thread mid-sentence and cannot finish, the words dissolving into a blank, frustrated silence.

In the weeks that followed, Kwame found himself flinching at the sound of footsteps behind him on the sidewalk. He started wearing hooded jackets and loose, dark clothing even in warm weather, hoping to blend in and avoid being noticed. He began avoiding unfamiliar neighborhoods entirely, because he could not assess the danger in a place he did not know. These habits made sense to him: if he was less visible, less out of place, he would not be targeted again. But the avoidance came with a cost. He stopped going to concerts, even though he used to love live music, because certain songs-especially ones with heavy bass or a pulsing beat-brought back the feeling of his heart hammering against the pavement. He also found himself dodging anything that reminded him of the friends he had lost touch with since the event, because their absence felt like another kind of grief he could not bear. He began avoiding all strong feelings, positive or negative, because every emotional spike felt like a warning.

The memory itself felt more real and vivid than ordinary memories. When it surfaced, he could hear the police radio in his head, the sharp static, the dispatcher's voice. He had come to believe that his life had been destroyed by that night. He used to be a happy person, he told himself, but now he was always miserable, always watching, always waiting. He was certain he was no longer capable of doing the things that defined him-his work as a journalist required him to go to unfamiliar places, to talk to strangers, to stay calm under pressure, and he could no longer do any of it without his concentration shattering. The sense that his life was ruined made the memory return more often, because every time he failed to function normally, the memory rushed in to remind him why.

At work, his editor noticed that Kwame had stopped volunteering for field assignments. He made excuses, but the truth was that every time he stepped outside, his attention narrowed to the threat around him. He frequently looked behind him to check if someone was following. The hypervigilance itself triggered more memories, because the act of scanning for danger replayed the sensory fragments of that night. And the memories, in turn, made the threat feel immediate and real again, so he checked behind him more often, and wore his hood tighter, and avoided more places.

The cycle tightened over months. Kwame's girlfriend grew worried and frustrated; she wanted to understand, but he could not explain. The more he withdrew, the more he believed he had lost himself for good. He finally sought help after a night when he heard footsteps on the stairs in his own building and spent an hour pressed against the wall of his apartment, certain the police were coming back. What frightened him most was the thought that this feeling would never lift-that the man he used to be was gone, and that all that remained was the vigilance and the silence.
